deep.reconstruction:
The page is a pure numerical table. It is page 11 of a continuous table that begins on earlier pages and continues on p.12. It has two blocks, argument 0.160–0.200 and 0.200–0.240, in steps of 0.001. There is no derivation on the page; what follows identifies the function from the numbers.

Each row reads: A | B | ΔB | C | ΔC.

(1) Column 3 is always column 1 plus column 2, i.e. C = A + B. Example: 0.160 + 0.22836 = 0.38836. Consequently each pair of tabular differences sums to 100 units of 1e-5 (41+59, 38+62, …).

(2) Identifying B (my reconstruction, verified numerically):
B(A) = log10(1 + 10^(-A)).
- At A = 0 this gives log10 2 = 0.30103, with slope -1/2. This matches extrapolation from the tabular differences.
- Recomputed at 8-digit precision, A = 0.170, 0.180, 0.190, 0.196, 0.210, 0.220, 0.230, 0.235, 0.236 and 0.240 give 0.22430, 0.22029, 0.21634, 0.21399 (0.2139944), 0.20860, 0.20481, 0.20108, 0.19923, 0.19887 and 0.19740 — all as written.

(3) It follows that C = A + B = log10(1 + 10^A).

So this is a 5-place table of Gaussian (addition/subtraction) logarithms. If a and b are numbers with log a − log b = A (a ≥ b), then:
- log(a + b) = log a + B = log b + C.
- For differences, the C column is entered inversely: log(a − b) is found by locating log a − log b in the C column.

The ΔB and ΔC columns are first differences in units of the fifth decimal, for linear interpolation. B is convex and decreasing; |ΔB| falls from 41 to 36 over this range, and ΔC rises correspondingly from 59 to 64.

The page continues seamlessly from p.10 (which ends at 0.160, 0.22836, 0.38836) into p.12 (which starts at 0.240, 0.19740, 0.43740).

The structure is: argument A, then B = log(1 + 1/a), then C = A + B, each with its differences. This is exactly the layout of Gauss's published table, 'Tafel zur bequemern Berechnung des Logarithmen der Summe oder Differenz zweier Grössen, welche selbst nur durch ihre Logarithmen gegeben sind' (Monatliche Correspondenz 26, 1812). The page is evidently manuscript material for, or a fair copy of, that table.
errors: No computational errors found. All recomputed spot values agree to the last (5th) place, and every printed difference is consistent with the adjacent tabular values. Borderline rounding cases (e.g. A=0.196, B=0.2139944) are correctly rounded.

results.what: 5-place table of B(A)=log10(1+10^-A) and C(A)=A+B=log10(1+10^A) for A=0.160..0.240, with first differences, for computing log(a±b) from log a and log b
results.usually_credited_to: Idea due to Z. Leonelli (Supplément logarithmique, 1802/03); popularized and tabulated by Gauss, Monatliche Correspondenz 1812, hence the name 'Gaussian logarithms'

deep.surprise_reason: These are the well-known Gaussian logarithms, which Gauss published in 1812. The page is a working or fair-copy sheet of that table, interesting only for dating (the bundle is labelled 1809) and as evidence of the computation process. No new mathematics.
